DOMESTIC VIOLENCE ACT 116 OF 1998, AS AMENDED (main sections used by inFORMed)
Summary in plain words, prepared for the legal advisor's review from the consolidated text of the Act (as amended by the Domestic Violence Amendment Act 14 of 2021, in force from 14 April 2023). Every point must be checked against the Act before this record is approved.

SECTION 1: KEY WORDS
- Child: a person under 18.
- Complainant: a person who is or was in a domestic relationship with the respondent and who is, or is said to be, experiencing domestic violence. It includes any child in the complainant's care.
- Domestic relationship: the complainant and respondent (a) are or were married, under any law, custom or religion; (b) live or lived together in a relationship like a marriage, of any sex, whether or not they are or could be married; (c) are or were parents of the same child, or have or had parental responsibility for that child; (d) are family by blood, marriage or adoption; (e) are or were engaged, dating, or in a customary relationship, including a real or perceived romantic, intimate or sexual relationship of any length; or (f) are in a close relationship and share or shared a residence.
- Close relationship: the court looks at the trust between them, how much they depend on and are committed to each other, how long the relationship has lasted, how often they are in contact, and how close they are.
- Related person: a member of the complainant's family or household, or someone in a close relationship with the complainant.
- Domestic violence: any of the following that harms the complainant or makes the complainant reasonably believe harm may be caused: physical abuse; sexual abuse; emotional, verbal or psychological abuse; economic abuse; intimidation; harassment; sexual harassment; related person abuse; spiritual abuse; damage to property; elder abuse; coercive behaviour; controlling behaviour; exposing a child to domestic violence; entering the complainant's home, work or place of study without consent where they do not share it; and any other intimidating, threatening, abusive, degrading, offensive or humiliating behaviour towards the complainant.
- Economic abuse: withholding money or resources the complainant is entitled to or needs (for example school costs, household necessities, bond or rent for the shared home); selling or getting rid of household things or property the complainant has an interest in, without permission; using the complainant's money without permission; forcing the complainant to give up control of income or assets, or to sign over the management of their finances.
- Coercive behaviour: forcing the complainant to stop doing something they are lawfully entitled to do, or to do something they are lawfully entitled not to do.
- Controlling behaviour: behaviour that makes the complainant dependent on or subservient to the respondent, for example cutting them off from support, using their resources or abilities for the respondent's gain, taking away what they need to be independent or to escape, and controlling their everyday life.
- Emergency monetary relief: (a) money lost because of the domestic violence up to the time of the order, for example lost earnings, medical, dental and optical costs, moving and accommodation costs, household necessities, education, transport and counselling costs; and (b) maintenance for a child, person with a disability or older person in the complainant's care whom the respondent must support, until a maintenance case is decided.

SECTION 2: WHAT THE POLICE MUST DO
At the scene, as soon as possible afterwards, or when the incident is reported, a police member must give the help the situation needs, including helping the complainant find a shelter and get medical treatment. Where reasonably possible, the member must give the complainant a notice with the prescribed information, in the official language the complainant chooses, and explain it, including the remedies under the Act and the right to lay a criminal complaint. A member who does not do this can be charged with misconduct (section 18(4)).

SECTION 2B: DUTY TO REPORT
An adult who knows, believes or reasonably suspects that domestic violence has been committed against a child, a person with a disability or an older person must report it as soon as possible to a social worker or the police, on the prescribed form, giving the reasons. Someone who reports in good faith is protected from legal and disciplinary action, and their identity can be kept confidential. Not reporting is an offence (fine or up to three months' imprisonment, section 17(4)). Functionaries have their own duties under section 2A.

SECTION 3: ARREST WITHOUT A WARRANT
A peace officer at the scene may arrest a respondent without a warrant if they reasonably suspect an act of domestic violence that is a crime, and must arrest without a warrant where they reasonably believe the respondent committed a violent crime against the complainant.

SECTION 4: APPLYING FOR A PROTECTION ORDER
- (1) Any complainant may apply to court, without the respondent being told first (ex parte), on the prescribed form. The application goes to the clerk of the court or the court's electronic address. An urgent application outside court hours or on a non-court day may go directly to the court.
- (2) If the applicant has no lawyer, the clerk must explain the relief available and the right to lay a criminal complaint if a crime was committed.
- (3) A functionary or another person with a material interest in the complainant's wellbeing may apply on the complainant's behalf, with the complainant's written consent. Consent is not needed if the complainant is a child and the court finds the application is in the child's best interests, or if the court finds the complainant cannot consent.
- (4) A child, or someone acting for a child, may apply without the consent or help of a parent, guardian or anyone else.
- (5) The court may consider an application outside court hours or on a non-court day if it shows that the complainant is suffering or may suffer harm unless it is dealt with immediately.
- (6) Supporting affidavits from people who know about the matter may be attached.
- (7) The clerk records the application in the integrated electronic repository and sends it to the court at once.

SECTION 5: INTERIM PROTECTION ORDER
- The court considers the application as soon as reasonably possible and may hear more evidence.
- Where a child may need care and protection, the court may ask for an investigation by the Family Advocate or a designated social worker.
- The court must give an interim protection order, even without telling the respondent, if there is prima facie evidence that the respondent is committing or has committed domestic violence, the complainant is suffering or may suffer harm, and an order is immediately necessary to protect them.
- The interim order and the application are served on the respondent by the clerk, sheriff or a peace officer, with a return date on which the respondent must show why the order should not be made final. The return date is at least 10 days after service.
- If no interim order is given, the application is still served, with a return date, and the clerk tells the complainant.
- The interim order takes effect once it has been served on the respondent, and stays in force until a court sets it aside. Certified copies of the order and the warrant of arrest go to the complainant and to the police station the complainant chose.

SECTION 6: FINAL PROTECTION ORDER
- If the respondent does not come to court on the return date after proper service, the court must give a final order where there is prima facie evidence of domestic violence (or, where no interim order was given, after hearing the matter and finding domestic violence on a balance of probabilities).
- If the respondent opposes, the court hears the matter and gives a final order if it finds, on a balance of probabilities, that domestic violence has been or is being committed. While facts are disputed, the interim order is extended.
- If the complainant does not come on the return date, the court may extend the interim order to a new date, and may later discharge it if the complainant still does not come.
- The court can stop a respondent without a lawyer from questioning the complainant directly; questions then go through the court.
- The final order is served on the respondent and takes effect once served. It stays in force until set aside; an appeal does not suspend it.

SECTION 7: WHAT THE COURT CAN ORDER
- The respondent can be ordered not to: commit or try to commit domestic violence; get someone else to do it; enter a shared residence (only where this is in the complainant's best interests) or a part of it; enter the complainant's home, workplace or place of study; stop the complainant from entering or staying in the shared residence; disclose or share electronic or other communications; or do any other act the order names.
- The court can add conditions needed for the complainant's safety, health or wellbeing, including seizing weapons, a peace officer going with the complainant to collect personal property, and recommending that the complainant report the matter to the police for possible prosecution.
- The court can order the respondent to pay rent or bond where he must stay out of a shared home, and emergency monetary relief.
- The court can send a respondent who appears to need treatment for substance abuse to an enquiry under the Prevention of and Treatment for Substance Abuse Act.
- The complainant's addresses and contact details are left out of the order unless they are needed, and the court can give directions to keep them from the respondent. A child's addresses are not disclosed until a children's court inquiry.
- Where it is in a child's best interests, the court can refuse the respondent contact with the child, or allow contact on conditions.
- The court may not refuse an order just because other legal remedies exist; where another law (for example the Maintenance Act) should deal with something, the court keeps the provision for a limited time so the person can apply under that law.

SECTION 8: WARRANT OF ARREST AND BREACH
- With every protection order, the court issues a warrant for the respondent's arrest, suspended as long as he obeys the order.
- If the order is breached, the complainant can give the warrant and an affidavit about the breach to the police. If the member reasonably suspects the complainant is suffering or may suffer harm, the member must arrest the respondent immediately; otherwise the member must give the respondent a written notice to appear in court.
- The police must tell the complainant of the right to lay a criminal charge at the same time, and explain how.
- If the warrant has been used, lost or destroyed, the clerk issues a new one on the complainant's affidavit.

SECTION 9: WEAPONS
The court must order the police to seize the respondent's weapons, even if he needs them for work, if he has threatened or intended to kill or injure himself or someone else, or if his having a weapon is not in anyone's interest because of his mental state, tendency to violence, or use of alcohol or drugs. After a final order, the police station commander must check his firearm licences and decide whether he is unfit to have a firearm.

SECTION 10: CHANGING OR CANCELLING AN ORDER
Either side can apply to change or set aside a final order, with written notice to the other side. The court does so only if circumstances have materially changed and there is good cause; it will not set aside an order at the complainant's request unless the complainant asks freely and voluntarily.

SECTION 11: PRIVACY
Only the people involved, their lawyers, witnesses, up to three supporters for each side, and others the court allows may attend. Nobody may publish anything that could identify the parties.

SECTION 12: WHICH COURT
Any magistrate's court where the complainant or the respondent lives, works, studies or does business, even temporarily, or where the abuse happened. There is no minimum time of living there. A protection order is valid everywhere in South Africa.

SECTION 13: SERVICE
Documents are served by the clerk, a sheriff or a peace officer. Where the parties live together, the documents must be handed to the person personally. People who cannot pay service fees can get help from the State, as the regulations set out.

SECTION 14: LAWYERS
Either side may have a lawyer. A lawyer is not required.

SECTION 17: OFFENCES
- Breaking a protection order: a fine or up to five years' imprisonment, or both (up to ten years for a second conviction).
- Publishing information that identifies the parties, or knowingly making a material false statement in an affidavit or declaration under the Act: a fine or up to two years' imprisonment, or both (up to four years for a second conviction).
- Not reporting under section 2B: a fine or up to three months' imprisonment, or both.
